newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien stays fiscal course in shuffle.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien stays fiscal course in shuffle.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, whose Liberal government was re-elected last week with a reduced majority, shuffled his cabinet on Wednesday but maintained his highly regarded economic team.

Chretien reappointed the tight-fisted Paul Martin as finance minister. Martin won international praise for slashing the Canadian budget deficit in the Liberals' first term and his reappointment had been eagerly sought by the markets.

"The economic team is totally unchanged," Chretien spokesman Peter Donolo told Reuters. "I think it's a very strong message about direction, about continuity, about seeing through the (deficit reduction) plan."
Donolo spoke at Rideau Hall -- the sumptuous residence of the Canadian representative of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, Canada's head of state -- where the cabinet was sworn in.
Chretien said in a statement the job of the new cabinet was "to complete the task of balancing the budget and putting Canada's finances on a sound and sustainable footing."

But in a possible signal the goverment would eventually increase spending on social programmes, he added it would seek to modernise and expand Canada's government-run health care system and "provide for the well-being of our children."

Chretien relieved left-leaning Heritage Minister Sheila Copps of her additional role as deputy prime minister, though he denied this was a demotion. Former government house leader Herb Gray succeeded Copps in the deputy prime minister's post.
In the aftermath of the June 2 election, in which the Liberals lost heavily in economically depressed Atlantic Canada, some Liberal legislators urged the party to veer to the left in a second term.
But Chretien reappointed John Manley -- viewed, like Martin, as a fiscal conservative -- as industry minister.
Justice Minister Allan Rock was moved to the health portfolio, a job that Copps had reportedly sought amid improving prospects for a budget surplus in coming years.
Chretien drew fire from both right and left over the economic direction of the government.

The Reform Party, who won the second largest number of seats partly because of its advocacy of lean government, said it was worried about remarks some Liberals have made since the election about the need to spend money again -- although little was said about this on Wednesday.
Reform leader Preston Manning said such remarks suggested "the government is declaring premature victory on budget balancing and shifting back toward tax-and-spend Liberalism."
Leftist New Democratic Party leader Alexa McDonough said the election's message was that more attention needed to be paid towards unemployment and that this was not heeded.

The Liberals lost two-thirds of their seats in economically depressed Atlantic Canada but also lost seats to Reform in the West. They took 155 of the 301 seats in the House of Commons, while Reform rose by eight to 60.

"There's nothing in the cabinet announced by the prime minister that would indicate that this government has listened, has heard, and intends to do things very differently," McDonough told a news conference.
Conservative Party leader Jean Charest said Chretien had yet to show why he had called an election, 1-1/2 years early.
The Chretien government shifted its focus on justice and social issues by appointing as justice minister Anne McLellan, who narrowly won re-election in the conservative western province of Alberta.
Her predecessor, Rock, angered conservative groups by tightening gun control and expanding rights for homosexuals.
Reform, which won most of the seats in Western Canada and came second in her district, campaigned on a tough law and order policy and most of its members are also conservative on social issues.
The new cabinet was expanded by two members to 36, including Chretien and junior ministers.
